anti_overlap: Leave Proposal/Debrief JSON-schema field design to fd-cross-codebase-schema-contract
Leave advisor-voice / annotation-vocabulary semantics to fd-advisor-proposal-loop
Leave Palettice 'taste/hands/lives' philosophy framing to fd-palettice-design-philosophy
decision_lens: Does the 6-stage lifecycle hold up as a state machine — distinct stages, well-defined transitions, no ambiguous overlaps, and graceful handling of nested local sub-stages (Gathering/Performing/Aftermath) without contradicting the shared shape?
focus: Six-stage culture-event lifecycle as a state machine: stage definitions, transitions, nesting semantics, and player-agency placement
name: fd-culture-event-lifecycle
persona: Apply the perspective of a culture-sim game designer who has shipped lifecycle-driven AI advisor loops — they care about whether each stage has a clear actor, a clear input, a clear output, and a clear failure mode. They measure clarity by asking 'what happens if a stage is skipped, repeated, or stalls?' and they flag any lifecycle whose transitions are implicit, ambiguous, or collapse under common gameplay scenarios.
review_areas: Stage definitions: are Prepare/Propose/Annotate/Event/Respond/Debrief each crisply distinguished by who acts and what artifact is produced?
Nesting semantics: how exactly does Elf Revel's Gathering→Performing→Aftermath nest inside the shared Event stage without leaking sub-state into Respond/Debrief?
Transition triggers: what causes each stage to advance — player input, sim tick, advisor output? Are any transitions left implicit?
Concurrency and re-entry: can a Proposal be re-annotated mid-Event? Can multiple culture-events overlap? Is the lifecycle per-event or per-colony?
Failure paths: what if the player ignores Annotate, rejects every proposal, or the Event aborts mid-Performing? Is degraded flow specified?
Mapping fidelity: does the doc actually show the UB Prep/Briefing/Notes/Event/Reaction/Debrief ↔ shared 6-stage correspondence, or is the generalization claimed but not demonstrated?

severity_examples.condition: If transition triggers and skip-behavior are not specified per stage, implementers in either game will diverge silently
severity_examples.scenario: Stage transitions are described as a linear arrow chain (Prepare → Propose → Annotate → ...) with no specification of what advances them or what happens when a player skips Annotate entirely

severity_examples.condition: If sub-stage visibility is ambiguous, downstream tooling (replay, eval) cannot tell whether to subscribe to local or shared events
severity_examples.scenario: Nested Event sub-stages (Gathering/Performing/Aftermath) are mentioned but the doc does not specify whether sub-stage transitions are visible to the shared layer or fully local

severity_examples.condition: Any stage in the canonical lifecycle without a definition undermines the spec's claim of being canonical
severity_examples.scenario: The 'Respond' stage is introduced as new but never defined — it appears in the diagram but no rationale, actor, or artifact is given

success_hints: Open by mapping each of the 6 stages to (actor, input, output, exit-trigger) — flag any row that cannot be filled in from the doc
Trace one concrete scenario end-to-end: e.g. 'patron ignores proposal, event runs anyway' — does the spec cover it?
Check whether the UB-side stage names (Prep/Briefing/Notes/Event/Reaction/Debrief) actually align 1:1 with the shared 6 stages, or whether the generalization papers over a mismatch
Flag any stage that exists in one game but is collapsed/absent in the other under the shared shape
task_context: Review the Revel Curator ↔ Underground Beets harmonization brainstorm with focus on whether the proposed 6-stage culture-event lifecycle (Prepare → Propose → Annotate → Event → Respond → Debrief) is well-defined as a shared state machine, whether stage nesting (Elf Revel's Gathering/Performing/Aftermath inside Event) is coherent, and whether transitions, failure modes, and sub-stage visibility are specified clearly enough for two independent implementations to converge on the same semantics.
